Causal inference using invariant prediction:
identification and confidence intervals

Jonas Peters Affiliation: MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen, Germany Affiliation: Seminar für Statistik, ETH Zürich, Switzerland Email: peters@stat.math.ethz.ch    Peter Bühlmann Affiliation: Seminar für Statistik, ETH Zürich, Switzerland Email: buhlmann@stat.math.ethz.ch    Nicolai Meinshausen Affiliation: Seminar für Statistik, ETH Zürich, Switzerland Email: meinshausen@stat.math.ethz.ch
Abstract

What is the difference of a prediction that is made with a causal model and a non-causal model? Suppose we intervene on the predictor variables or change the whole environment. The predictions from a causal model will in general work as well under interventions as for observational data. In contrast, predictions from a non-causal model can potentially be very wrong if we actively intervene on variables. Here, we propose to exploit this invariance of a prediction under a causal model for causal inference: given different experimental settings (for example various interventions) we collect all models that do show invariance in their predictive accuracy across settings and interventions. The causal model will be a member of this set of models with high probability. This approach yields valid confidence intervals for the causal relationships in quite general scenarios. We examine the example of structural equation models in more detail and provide sufficient assumptions under which the set of causal predictors becomes identifiable. We further investigate robustness properties of our approach under model misspecification and discuss possible extensions. The empirical properties are studied for various data sets, including large-scale gene perturbation experiments.

1 Introduction

Inferring cause-effect relationships between variables is a primary goal in many applications. Such causal inference has its roots in different fields and various concepts have contributed to its understanding and quantification. Among them are the framework of potential outcomes and counterfactuals (Dawid, 2000; Rubin, 2005, cf.); or structural equation modelling (Bollen, 1989; Robins et al., 2000; Pearl, 2009, cf.) and graphical modeling (Lauritzen and Spiegelhalter, 1988; Greenland et al., 1999; Spirtes et al., 2000, cf.), where the book by Pearl (2009) provides a nice overview. Richardson and Robins (2013) make a connection between the frameworks using single-world intervention graphs.

A typical approach for causal discovery, in the context of unknown causal structure, is to characterise the Markov equivalence class of structures (or graphs) (Verma and Pearl, 1991; Andersson et al., 1997; Tian and Pearl, 2001; Hauser and Bühlmann, 2012), estimate the correct Markov equivalence class based on observational or interventional data (Spirtes et al., 2000; Chickering, 2002; Castelo and Kocka, 2003; Kalisch and Bühlmann, 2007; He and Geng., 2008; Hauser and Bühlmann, 2015, cf.), and finally infer the identifiable causal effects or provide some bounds (Maathuis et al., 2009; VanderWeele and Robins, 2010, cf.). More recently, within the framework of structural equation models, interesting work has been done for fully identifiable structures exploiting additional restrictions such as non-Gaussianity (Shimizu et al., 2006), nonlinearity (Hoyer et al., 2009; Peters et al., 2014) or equal error variances (Peters and Bühlmann, 2014). Janzing et al. (2012) exploit an independence between causal mechanisms.

We propose here a new method for causal discovery. The approach of the paper is to note that if we consider all ‘‘direct causes’’ of a target variable of interest, then the conditional distribution of the target given the the direct causes will not change when we interfere experimentally with all other variables in the model except the target itself. This does not necessarily hold, however, if some of the direct causes are ignored in the conditioning.11 1 We thank a referee for suggesting this succinct description of the main idea. We exploit, in other words, that the conditional distribution of the target variable of interest (often also termed “response variable”), given the complete set of corresponding direct causal predictors, has to remain identical under interventions on variables other than the target variable. This invariance idea is closely linked to causality and has been discussed, for example, under the term “autonomy” and “modularity” (Haavelmo, 1944; Aldrich, 1989; Hoover, 1990; Pearl, 2009; Schölkopf et al., 2012) or also “stability” (Dawid and Didelez, 2010) (Pearl, 2009, Sec. 1.3.2). While it is well-known that causal models have an invariance property, we try to exploit this fact for inference. Our proposed procedure gathers all submodels that are statistically invariant across environments in a suitable sense. The causal submodel consisting of the set of variables with a direct causal effect on the target variable will be one of these invariant submodels, with controlled high probability, and this allows to control the probability of making false causal discoveries.

Our method is tailored for (but not restricted to) the setting where we have data from different experimental settings or regimes (Didelez et al., 2006). For example, two different interventional data samples, or a combination of observational and interventional data (He and Geng., 2008, cf.) belong to such a scenario. For known intervention targets, Cooper and Yoo (1999) incorporate the intervention effects as mechanism changes (Tian and Pearl, 2001) into a Bayesian framework and Hauser and Bühlmann (2015) modify the greedy equivalence search (Chickering, 2002) for perfect interventions. Our framework does not require to know the location of interventions. For this setting, Eaton and Murphy (2007) use intervention nodes with unknown children and Tian and Pearl (2001) consider changes in marginal distributions, while Dawid (2012); Dawid (2015) make use of different regimes for a decision-theoretic approach. In contrast to these approaches, our framework does not require the fitting of graphical, structural equation or potential outcome models and comes with statistical guarantees. Further advantages are indicated below in Section 1.2.

We primarily consider the situation with no hidden (confounder) variables that influence the target variable. A rigorous treatment with hidden variables would be more involved (see Richardson and Spirtes, 2002, for graphical language) but we provide an example with instrumental variables in Section 5 to illustrate that the method could also work more generally in the context of hidden variables. We do not touch very much on the framework of feedback models (Lauritzen and Richardson, 2002; Mooij et al., 2011; Hyttinen et al., 2012, cf.), although a constrained form of feedback is allowed. It is an open question whether our approach could be generalised to include general feedback models.

1.1 Data from multiple environments or experimental settings

We consider the setting where we have different experimental conditions e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} and have an i.i.d. sample of (Xe,Ye)(X^{e},Y^{e}) in each environment, where Xe∈ℝpX^{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a predictor variable and Ye∈ℝY^{e}\in\mathbb{R} a target variable of interest. While the environments e∈ℰe\in{\mathcal{E}} can be created by precise experimental design for XeX^{e} (for example by randomising some or all elements of XeX^{e}), we are more interested in settings where such careful experimentation is not possible and the different distributions of XeX^{e} in the environments are generated by unknown and not precisely controlled interventions. If a subset S∗⊆{1,…,p}S^{*}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} is causal for the prediction of a response YY, we assume that

Ye=g⁡(XS∗e,εe),εe∼Fε​ and ​εe​⟂⁣⟂​XS∗e,\displaystyle Y^{e}=g(X^{e}_{S^{*}},\varepsilon^{e}),\quad\varepsilon^{e}\sim F_{\varepsilon}\mbox{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}X^{e}_{S^{*}}, (2)

Equations (1) and (2) can also be interpreted as requiring that the conditionals Ye|XS∗eY^{e}\,|\,X^{e}_{S^{*}} and Yf|XS∗fY^{f}\,|\,X^{f}_{S^{*}} are identical for all environments e,f∈ℰe,f\in{\mathcal{E}} (this equivalence is proved in Section 6.1).

An example of a set of environments can be seen in Figure 1. The invariance (1) and (2) holds if the set S∗S^{*} consists of all direct causes of the target variable YY and if we do not intervene on YY, see Proposition 1.

Sections 5, 6.2 and 6.3 discuss violations and possible relaxations of this assumption.

1.2 New contribution

The main and novel idea is that we can use the invariance of the causal relationships under different settings e∈ℰe\in{\mathcal{E}} for statistical estimation, which opens a new road for causal discovery and inference.

For the sake of simplicity, we will mostly focus on a linear model with a target or response variable and various predictor variables, where Equation (1) is unchanged and (2) then reads Ye=μ+Xe​γ∗+εeY^{e}=\mu+X^{e}\gamma^{*}+\varepsilon^{e}, with μ\mu a constant intercept term. The set S∗S^{*} of predictors is then given by the support of γ∗\gamma^{*}, that is S∗:={k;γk∗≠0}S^{*}:=\{k;\ \gamma^{*}_{k}\neq 0\}. Assumption 1 in Section 2 summarises all requirements. Proposition 1 shows that structural equation models with the traditional notion of interventions (Pearl, 2009) satisfy Assumption 1 if we choose the set S∗S^{*} to be the parents of YY. Proposition 6 in Appendix D sheds some light on the relationship to potential outcomes.

Obtaining confidence statements for existing causal discovery methods is often difficult as one would need to determine the distribution of causal effects estimators after having searched and estimated a graphical structure of the model. It is unknown how one could do this, except relying on data-splitting strategies which have been found to perform rather poorly in such a setting (Bühlmann et al., 2013). We propose in Section 3 a new method for the construction of (potentially) conservative confidence statements for causal predictors S∗S^{*} and of (potentially) conservative intervals for γj∗\gamma^{*}_{j} for j=1,…,pj=1,\ldots,p without a-priori knowing or assuming a causal ordering of variables. The method provides confidence intervals without relying on assumptions such as faithfulness or other identifiability assumptions. If a causal effect is not identifiable from the given data, it would automatically detect this fact and not make false causal discoveries.

Another main advantage of our methodology is that we do not need to know how the experimental conditions arise or which type of interventions they induce. We only assume that the intervention does not change the conditional distribution of the target given the causal predictors (no intervention on the target or a hidden confounder): it is simply a device exploiting the grouping of data into blocks, where every block corresponds to an experimental condition e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. We will show in Section 3.2 that such grouping can be misspecified and the coverage statements are still correct. This is again a major bonus in practice as it is often difficult to specify what an intervention or change of environment actually means. In contrast, for a so-called do-intervention for structural equation models (Pearl, 2009) it needs to be specified on which variables it acts. Interesting areas of applications include studies where observational data alone are not sufficient to infer causal effects but randomised studies are infeasible to conduct.

We believe that the method’s underlying invariance principle is rather general. However, for simplicity, we present our main results for linear Gaussian models, including some settings with instrumental variables and hidden variables.

1.3 Organization

The invariance assumption is formulated and discussed in Section 2. Using this invariance assumption, a general way to construct confidence statements for causal predictors and associated coefficients is derived in Section 3. Two specific methods are shown, using regression effects for various sets of predictors as the main ingredient. Identifiability results for structural equation models are given in Section 4. The relation to instrumental variables and the behaviour in presence of hidden variables is discussed in Section 5. We will discuss extensions to the nonlinear model (2) in Section 6.1 and extenstions to intervened targets in Section 6.2. Some robustness property against model misspecifications is discussed in Section 6.3.

Simulations and applications to a biological gene perturbation data set and an educational study related to instrumental variables are presented in Section 7. We discuss the results and provide an outlook in Section 8.

1.4 Software

The methods are available in the package InvariantCausalPrediction for the R-language (R Core Team, 2014).

2 Assumed invariance of causal prediction

We formulate here the invariance assumption and discuss the notion of identifiable causal predictors. Let ℰ{\mathcal{E}} denote again the index set of |ℰ||{\mathcal{E}}| possible interventional or experimental settings. As stated above, we have variables (Xe,Ye)(X^{e},Y^{e}) with a joint distribution that will in general depend on the environment e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. In the simplest case, |ℰ|=2|{\mathcal{E}}|=2, and we have for example in the first setting observational data and interventions of some (possibly unknown) nature in the second setting.

Our discussion will rest on the following assumption. We assume the existence of a model that is invariant under different experimental or intervention settings. Let for any set S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}, XSX_{S} be the vector containing all variables Xk,k∈SX_{k},k\in S.

Assumption 1 (Invariant prediction)

There exists a vector of coefficients γ∗=(γ1∗,…,γp∗)t\gamma^{*}=(\gamma^{*}_{1},\ldots,\gamma^{*}_{p})^{t} with support S∗:={k:γk∗≠0}⊆{1,…,p}S^{*}:=\{k:\gamma^{*}_{k}\neq 0\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} that satisfies

for all ​e∈ℰ:\displaystyle\mbox{for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}:\quad Xe​ has an arbitrary distribution  and\displaystyle X^{e}\mbox{ has an arbitrary distribution }\mbox{ and }
Ye=μ+Xe​γ∗+εe,εe∼Fε​ and ​εe​⟂⁣⟂​XS∗e,\displaystyle Y^{e}=\mu+X^{e}\gamma^{*}+\varepsilon^{e},\quad\varepsilon^{e}\sim F_{\varepsilon}\mbox{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}X_{S^{*}}^{e}, (3)

where μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R} is an intercept term, εe\varepsilon^{e} is random noise with mean zero, finite variance and the same distribution FεF_{\varepsilon} across all e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}.

The distribution FεF_{\varepsilon} is not assumed to be known in general. If not mentioned otherwise, we will always assume that an intercept μ\mu is added to the model (3). To simplify notation, we will from now on refrain from writing the intercept down explicitly. We discuss the invariance assumption with the help of some examples in Figure 1 and 2; see also Appendix A for another artificial example.

We observe each unit ii in only one experimental setting. The distribution of the error εe\varepsilon^{e} is assumed to stay identical across all environments (though see Sections 6.2 and 6.3 for approaches when this assumption is violated). It is in general not possible to estimate the correlation between the noise variables εie\varepsilon^{e}_{i} and εif\varepsilon^{f}_{i} for a single unit ii in different hypothetical environments ee and ff, as the outcome is observed for only one environment (Dawid, 2006; Dawid, 2012). Knowledge of the correlation would be necessary to answer counterfactual questions about the outcome. Knowledge of the correlation is not necessary for our method.

We deliberately avoid the term “causality” in Assumption 1 in order to keep it purely mathematical. Proposition 1 establishes a link to causality by showing that the parents of YY in a structural equation model (SEM) satisfy Assumption 1. In other words, the variables that have a direct causal effect on YY in a SEM form a set S∗S^{*} for which Assumption 1 is satisfied. This must not necessarily be true for the variables that have an (in)direct effect on YY, i.e., the ancestors of YY. However, the set S∗S^{*} is not necessarily unique. For a given set of experimental conditions ℰ{\mathcal{E}}, there can be multiple vectors γ∗\gamma^{*} that satisfy (3). For example, if only observational data are available, i.e. all environments are identical, it is apparent that for any model (3) the distribution FεF_{\varepsilon} of the residuals εe\varepsilon^{e} does not depend on ee. If additionally (X,Y)(X,Y) have a joint Gaussian distribution and XX and YY are not independent, for example, then one can find a solution γ∗\gamma^{*} to (3) for every subset S∗⊆{1,…,p}S^{*}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}. The inference we propose works for any possible choice among the set of solutions. We can at most identify the subset of S∗S^{*} that is common among all possible solutions of (3), see Section 4 for settings with complete identifiability.

It is perhaps easiest to think about the example of a linear structural equation model (SEM), as defined in Section 4.1, see also Figure 8 in Appendix A. We show in the following proposition that the set of parents of YY in a linear SEM is a valid set S∗S^{*} satisfying (3).

Proposition 1

Consider a linear structural equation model, as formally defined in Section 4.1, for the variables (X1=Y,X2,…,Xp,Xp+1)(X_{1}=Y,X_{2},\ldots,X_{p},X_{p+1}), with coefficients (βj​k)j,k=1,…,p+1(\beta_{jk})_{j,k=1,\ldots,p+1}, whose structure is given by a directed acyclic graph. The independence assumption on the noise variables in Section 4.1 can here be replaced by the strictly weaker assumption that ε1e​⟂⁣⟂​{εje;j∈𝐀𝐍⁡(1)}\varepsilon^{e}_{1}\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}\{\varepsilon^{e}_{j};j\in{\mathbf{AN}}{(1)}\} for all environments e∈ℰe\in{\mathcal{E}}, where 𝐀𝐍⁡(1){\mathbf{AN}}{(1)} are the ancestors of YY. Then Assumption 1 holds for the parents of YY, namely S∗=𝐏𝐀⁡(1)S^{*}={\mathbf{PA}}{(1)}, and γ∗=β1,⋅\gamma^{*}=\beta_{1,\cdot} as defined in Section 4.1, under the following assumption:

for each e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}: the experimental setting e{e} arises by one or several interventions on variables from {X2,…,Xp+1}\{X_{2},\ldots,X_{p+1}\} but interventions on YY are not allowed; here, we allow for do-interventions (Pearl, 2009) (see also Section 4.2.1, and note that the assigned values can be random, too), or soft-interventions (Eberhardt and Scheines, 2007) (see also Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3).

Proof. It follows by the definition of the interventions in Section 4.2 and because the interventions do not act on the target variable YY, that Ye=∑j∈𝐏𝐀⁡(1)β1,j​Xje+εYeY^{e}=\sum_{j\in{\mathbf{PA}}{(1)}}\beta_{1,j}X_{j}^{e}+\varepsilon_{Y}^{e} for all e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}, where εYe=ε1e\varepsilon_{Y}^{e}=\varepsilon_{1}^{e} is independent of X𝐏𝐀⁡(1)X_{{\mathbf{PA}}{(1)}} and has the same distribution for all e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. Thus, Assumption 1 holds. □\square

We remark that Proposition 1 can be generalised to include some hidden variables: the exact statement is given in Proposition 4 in Appendix B.

Instead of allowing only do- or soft-interventions in Proposition 1, we can allow for more general interventions which could change the structural equations for X2,…,Xp+1X_{2},\ldots,X_{p+1} (including for example a change in the graphical structure of the model among the variables X2,…,Xp+1X_{2},\ldots,X_{p+1}), as long as the conditional distribution of YeY^{e} given XS∗eX_{S^{*}}^{e} remains the same. Such a weaker requirement is sometimes referred to as “modularity” (Pearl, 2009) or what is called “autonomy” (Haavelmo, 1944; Aldrich, 1989); structural equations are autonomous if whenever we replace one of them due to an intervention, all other structural equations do not change, they remain invariant. The remaining part of the condition in Proposition 1 about excluding interventions on the target variable YY is often verifiable in many applications; see Sections 6.2 and 6.3 for violations of this assumption.

Proposition 1 refers to standard linear SEMs that do not allow for feedback cycles. We may, however, include feedback into the SEM and consider equilibrium solutions of the new set of equations. The independence assumption between εe\varepsilon^{e} and XS∗eX_{S^{*}}^{e} allows for some feedback cycles in the linear SEM. The independence assumption prohibits, however, cycles that include the target variable YY. We will leave it as an open question to what extent the approach can be generalised to more general forms of feedback models.

It is noteworthy that our inference is valid for any set that satisfies Assumption 1 and not only parents in a linear SEM. For the following statements we do not specify whether the set S∗S^{*} refers to the set of parents in a linear SEM or any other set that satisfies (3), as the confidence guarantees will be valid in either case. Proposition 6 in Appendix D discusses some relationship to the potential outcome framework.

2.2 Plausible causal coefficients

We have seen that the null hypothesis (4) H0,γ,S​(ℰ)H_{0,\gamma,S}({\mathcal{E}}) is in general not only fulfilled for γ∗\gamma^{*} and its support S∗S^{*} but also potentially for other vectors γ∈ℝp\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{p}. This is true especially if the experimental settings ℰ{\mathcal{E}} are very similar to each other. If we consider again the extreme example of just a single environment, |ℰ|=1|{\mathcal{E}}|=1, and a multivariate Gaussian distribution for (X,Y)(X,Y), we can find for any set S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} a vector γ\gamma with support SS that fulfills the null hypothesis H0,γ,S​(ℰ)H_{0,\gamma,S}({\mathcal{E}}), namely by using the regression coefficient when regressing YY on XSX_{S}. If the interventions that produce the environments ℰ{\mathcal{E}} are stronger and we have more of those environments, the set of vectors that fulfill the null becomes smaller. We call vectors that fulfill the null hypothesis plausible causal coefficients.

The global set of plausible causal coefficients Γ⁡(ℰ)\Gamma({\mathcal{E}}) is, in other words, shrinking as we enlarge the set ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of possible experimental settings.

The null hypothesis H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) in (5) can be simplified. Writing

βpred,e(S):=argminβ∈ℝp:βk=0​ if ​k∉SE(Ye−Xeβ)2\beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S)\;:=\;\mbox{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\beta_{k}=0\text{ if }k\notin S}\;E(Y^{e}-X^{e}\beta)^{2} (9)

for the least-squares population regression coefficients when regressing the target of interest onto the variables in SS in experimental setting e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}, we obtain the equivalent formulation of the null hypothesis for set S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\},

H0,S(ℰ):{∃β∈ℝp​ and ​∃Fε​ such that for all ​e∈ℰ​ we have βpred,e(S)≡β and Ye=Xeβ+εe, where εe⟂⁣⟂XeS and εe∼Fε.\displaystyle H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}):\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\text{ and }\exists F_{\varepsilon}\mbox{ such that for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}\text{ we have }\\ \beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S)\equiv\beta\mbox{ and }Y^{e}=X^{e}\beta+\varepsilon^{e},\mbox{ where }\varepsilon^{e}\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}X^{e}_{S}\mbox{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\sim F_{\varepsilon}.\end{array}\right.

We conclude that

ΓS​(ℰ)={∅if ​H0,S​(ℰ)​ is falseβpred,e​(S)otherwise.{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\emptyset&\mbox{if }H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\mbox{ is false}\\ \beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S)&\mbox{otherwise}.\end{array}\right. (12)

In other words, the set of plausible causal coefficients for a set SS is either empty or contains only the population regression vector. We will make use of this fact further below in Section 3 when computing empirical estimators.

3 Estimation of identifiable causal predictors

We would like to estimate the set S⁡(ℰ)S({\mathcal{E}}) of identifiable causal predictors (6) when observing the distribution of (Xe,Ye)(X^{e},Y^{e}) under different experimental conditions e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. At the same time, we might be interested in obtaining confidence intervals for the linear causal coefficients.

Recall again the definition (5) of the null hypothesis H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}). Suppose for the moment that a statistical test for H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) with size smaller than a significance level α\alpha is available. Then the construction of an estimator S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) and confidence sets Γ^​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}}) for the causal coefficients can work as follows.

1) For each set S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}, test whether H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) holds at level α\alpha (we will discuss later concrete examples). 2) Set S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) as S^(ℰ):=⋂S:H0,S​(ℰ)​ not rejectedS.\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\;:=\;\bigcap_{S:H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ not rejected}}S. (13) 3) For the confidence sets, define Γ^​(ℰ):=⋃S⊆{1,…,p}Γ^S​(ℰ),\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}}):=\bigcup_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}}\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}), (14) where Γ^S​(ℰ):={∅H0,S​(ℰ)​ can be rejected at level αC^​(S)otherwise.\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}})\;:=\;\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\emptyset&H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\mbox{ can be rejected at level $\alpha$}\\ \hat{C}(S)&\mbox{otherwise}.\end{array}\right. (15) Here, C^​(S)\hat{C}(S) is a (1−α)(1-\alpha)-confidence set for the regression vector βpred​(S)\beta^{\mathrm{pred}}(S) that is obtained by pooling the data.

As an example, consider again Figure 2. Taking the example in the bottom left panel, we cannot reject H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) for S={YPL273W}S=\{\mathit{YPL273W}\}. Hence we can see already from this plot that S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) is either empty or that S^​(ℰ)={YPL273W}\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\{\mathit{YPL273W}\}. The latter case happens if no further set of variables is accepted that does not include the activity of gene YPL273W\mathit{YPL273W} as predictor.

A justification for pooling the data in (15) is given in Section 3.2. (The construction is also valid if the confidence set is based only on data from a single environment, but a confidence set for the pooled data will be smaller in general.) This defines a whole family of estimators and confidence sets as we have flexibility in the test we are using for the null hypothesis (5) and how the confidence interval C^​(S)\hat{C}(S) is constructed.

If the test and pooled confidence interval have the claimed size and coverage probability, we can guarantee coverage of the true causal predictors and the true causal coefficient, as shown below in Theorem 1.

Theorem 1

Assume that the estimator S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) is constructed according to (13) with a valid test for H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) for all sets S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} at level α\alpha in the sense that for all SS, supP:H0,S​(ℰ)​ trueP[H0,S(ℰ) rejected]≤α\sup_{P\,:\,H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ true}}\;P[H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ rejected}]\leq\nolinebreak\alpha. Consider now a distribution PP over (Y,X)(Y,X) and consider any γ∗\gamma^{*} and S∗S^{*} such that Assumption 1 holds. Then, S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) satisfies

P[S^(ℰ)⊆S∗]≥ 1−α.P\big[\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\subseteq S^{*}\big]\geq\;1-\alpha.

If, moreover, for all (γ,S)(\gamma,S) that satisfy Assumption 1, the confidence set C^​(S)\hat{C}(S) in (15) satisfies P[γ∈C^(S)]≥1−αP[\gamma\in\hat{C}(S)]\geq 1-\alpha then the set Γ^​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}}) (14) has coverage at least level 1−2​α1-2\alpha:

P[γ∗∈Γ^(ℰ)]≥ 1−2α.P\big[\gamma^{*}\in\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}})\big]\geq\;1-2\alpha.

Proof. The first property follows immediately since

P[S^(ℰ)⊆S∗]=P[⋂S:H0,S​(ℰ)​ not rejectedS⊆S∗]≥P[H0,S∗(ℰ) not rejected]≥ 1−α,\displaystyle P\big[\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\subseteq S^{*}\big]\;=\;P\Big[\bigcap_{S:H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ not rejected}}S\subseteq S^{*}\Big]\;\geq\;P\big[H_{0,S^{*}}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ not rejected}\big]\;\geq\;1-\alpha,

where the last inequality follows by the assumption that the test for H0,SH_{0,S} is valid at level α\alpha for all sets S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}. The second property follows since

P[γ∗∉Γ^(ℰ)]≤P[H0,S∗(ℰ) rejected or γ∗∉C^(S∗)]≤α+α=2α.P\big[\gamma^{*}\notin\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}})\big]\;\leq\;P\big[H_{0,S^{*}}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ rejected or }\gamma^{*}\notin\hat{C}(S^{*})\big]\;\leq\;\alpha+\alpha=2\alpha.

□\square

The confidence sets thus have the correct (conservative) coverage. The estimator of the causal predictors will, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, not erroneously include non-causal predictors. Note that the statement is true for any set of experimental or intervention settings. In the worst case, the set S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) might be empty but the error control is valid nonetheless.

Since Theorem 1 holds for any γ∗,S∗\gamma^{*},S^{*} which fulfil Assumption 1, and assuming the setting of Proposition 1, we obtain the corresponding confidence statements for the causal coefficients and causal variables in a linear structural equation model, that is for γ∗=β1,⋅\gamma^{*}=\beta_{1,\cdot} and S∗=𝐏𝐀⁡(1)S^{*}={\mathbf{PA}}{(1)} in the notation of Proposition 1.

Remark 1
  • (i)

    We obtain the following empirical version of (6):

    S^(ℰ)=⋂γ∈Γ^​(ℰ){k:γk≠0}=⋂S:H0,S​(ℰ)​ not rejected at ​αS\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\;=\;\bigcap_{\gamma\in\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}})}\{k:\gamma_{k}\neq 0\}\;=\;\bigcap_{S:{H}_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ not rejected at }\alpha}S (16)

    provided that if H0,S​(ℰ){H}_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) is not rejected, then for all γ∈Γ^S​(ℰ)\gamma\in\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}) we have supp⁡(γ)⊆S\mathrm{supp}(\gamma)\subseteq S and H0,supp⁡(γ)​(ℰ)H_{0,\mathrm{supp}(\gamma)}({\mathcal{E}}) is not rejected either.

  • (ii)

    In (15), we have constructed confidence sets Γ^S​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}) based on a test for H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}). Alternatively, confidence sets Γ^S​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}) may be available that are not based on a test procedure for H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}). In this case, we may take them as a starting point and define S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) using the first equality in (16), instead of (13). Analogously to Theorem 1, the correct coverage property of Γ^S∗​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}_{S^{*}}({\mathcal{E}}) then implies confidence statements for Γ^​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}({\mathcal{E}}) and S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}).

3.1 Two concrete proposals

The missing piece in the generic procedure given by (13) and (14) is a test for H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) that is valid at level α\alpha for any given set of variables S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} and thus implies

P⁡[H0,S∗​(ℰ)​ rejected]≤α.P\big[H_{0,S^{*}}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ rejected}\big]\leq\alpha.

To specify a concrete procedure and derive its statistical properties, we assume throughout the paper that the data consist of nn independent observations. Within each experimental setting ee, we assume that we receive nen_{{e}} independent and identically distributed data points from (Xe,Ye)(X^{e},Y^{e}) and thus, ∑e∈ℰne=n\sum_{{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}}n_{{e}}=n.

We now propose a way to construct such a test, but acknowledge that different choices are possible. Our construction will be based on the fact that the causal coefficients are identical to the regression effects in all experimental settings e∈ℰe\in{\mathcal{E}} if we consider only variables in the set S∗S^{*} of causal predictors.

For experimental setting e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} and a subset SS of variables, define the regression coefficients βpred,e​(S)∈ℝp\beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S)\in\mathbb{R}^{p} as above in (9). Define further the population residual standard deviations when regressing YeY^{e} on variables XSeX_{S}^{e} as

σe​(S)\displaystyle\sigma^{e}(S)\; :=[E​(Ye−Xe​βpred,e​(S))2]1/2.\displaystyle:=[E(Y^{e}-X^{e}\beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S))^{2}]^{1/2}.

These definitions are population quantities. The corresponding sample quantities are denoted with a hat. As mentioned above, under Assumption 1, for S=S∗S=S^{*}, the regression effects are identical to the causal coefficients: for all e∈Ee\in E,

βpred,e​(S∗)≡γ∗andσe​(S∗)≡Var​(Fε)1/2.\beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S^{*})\equiv\gamma^{*}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\sigma^{e}(S^{*})\equiv{\mathrm{Var}}(F_{\varepsilon})^{1/2}.

To get a test valid at level α\alpha for all subsets SS of predictor variables, we first weaken H0,S​(ℰ)H_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) in (2.2) to

H~0,S(ℰ):∃(β,σ)∈ℝp×ℝ+ such that βpred,e(S)≡β and σe(S)≡σ for all e∈ℰ.\tilde{H}_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}):\quad\exists(\beta,\sigma)\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\mbox{ such that }\beta^{\mathrm{pred},{e}}(S)\equiv\beta\mbox{ and }\sigma^{e}(S)\equiv\sigma\mbox{ for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. (17)

The null hypothesis H~0,S​(ℰ)\tilde{H}_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) is true whenever the original null hypothesis (2.2) is true. As in (15), we set

Γ^S​(ℰ):={∅H~0,S​(ℰ)​ can be rejected at level αC^​(S)otherwise.\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\emptyset&\tilde{H}_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}})\mbox{ can be rejected at level $\alpha$}\\ \hat{C}(S)&\mbox{otherwise}.\end{array}\right.

We now give a concrete example which we will use in the numerical examples under the assumption of Gaussian errors and that the design matrix 𝐗e\mathbf{X}_{e} of all nen_{e} samples in experimental setting e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} has full rank. (We write the design matrix in bold letters, as opposed to the random variables XeX^{e}.) The whole procedure is then a specific version of the general procedure given further above, where we use a specific test in the first step (the second step is unchanged).

1) For each S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} and e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}: (a) Let IeI_{e} with ne=|Ie|n_{e}=|I_{e}| be the set of observations where experimental setting e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} was active. Likewise, let I−e={1,…,n}∖IeI_{-{e}}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus I_{e} with n−e:=|I−e|n_{-{e}}:=|I_{-{e}}| be the set of observations when using only observations where experimental setting e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} was not active. Let 𝐗e,S\mathbf{X}_{{e},S} be the ne×(1+|S|)n_{e}\times(1+|S|)-dimensional matrix when using all samples in IeI_{e} and all predictor variables in SS, adding an intercept term to the design matrix as mentioned previously. If S=∅S=\emptyset, the matrix consists only of a single intercept column. Analogously, 𝐗−e,S\mathbf{X}_{-e,S} is defined with the samples in I−eI_{-{e}}. Let Y^e\hat{Y}_{e} be the predictions for observations in set IeI_{e} when using the OLS estimator computed on samples in I−eI_{-{e}} and let D:=Ye−Y^eD:=Y_{e}-\hat{Y}_{e} be the difference between the actual observations YeY_{e} on IeI_{e} and the predictions. (b) Under Gaussian errors, if (17) is true for a set SS, then (Chow, 1960) Dt​ΣD−1​Dσ^2​ne∼F⁡(ne,n−e−|S|−1),\frac{D^{t}\Sigma_{D}^{-1}D}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}\,n_{e}}\sim\;F(n_{e},n_{-{e}}-|S|-1), (18) where σ^2\hat{\sigma}^{2} is the estimated variance on the set I−eI_{-{e}} on which the OLS estimator is computed. The covariance matrix ΣD\Sigma_{D} is given by ΣD=1ne+𝐗e,S​(𝐗−e,St​𝐗−e,S)−1​𝐗e,St,\Sigma_{D}={1}_{n_{e}}+\mathbf{X}_{{e},S}(\mathbf{X}_{-{e},S}^{t}\mathbf{X}_{-{e},S})^{-1}\mathbf{X}_{{e},S}^{t}, letting 1n1_{n} be the identity matrix in nn-dimensions. For any set SS, we reject the null hypothesis H~0,S​(ℰ)\tilde{H}_{0,S}({\mathcal{E}}) if the pp-value of (18) is below α/|ℰ|\alpha/|{\mathcal{E}}| for any e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. 2) As in the generic algorithm, using (13). 3) If we do reject a set SS we set Γ^S​(ℰ)=∅\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\emptyset. Otherwise, we set Γ^S​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}) to be a (1−α)(1-\alpha)-confidence interval for βpred​(S)\beta^{\mathrm{pred}}(S) when using all data simultaneously. For simplicity, we will use a rectangular confidence region where the constraint for βpred​(S)k\beta^{\mathrm{pred}}(S)_{k} is identically 0 if k∉Sk\notin S and for coefficients in SS given by (β^pred​(S))S±t1−α/(2​|S|),n−|S|−1⋅σ^​diag​((𝐗St​𝐗S)−1)(\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{pred}}(S))_{S}\pm t_{1-\alpha/(2|S|),n-|S|-1}\cdot\hat{\sigma}\,\mbox{diag}((\mathbf{X}_{S}^{t}\mathbf{X}_{S})^{-1}), where 𝐗S\mathbf{X}_{S} is the design matrix of the pooled data when using variables in SS, t1−α;qt_{1-\alpha;q} is the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of a t-distribution with qq degrees of freedom, and σ^2\hat{\sigma}^{2} the estimated residual variance.

A justification of the pooling in step 3 is given in Section 3.2. The procedure above has some shortcomings. For example, the inversion of the covariance matrix in (18) might be too slow if we have to search many sets and the sample size is large. One can then just work with a random subsample of the set IeI_{e} of size, say, a few hundred, to speed up the computation. It also depends on the assumption of Gaussian errors, although this could be addressed by using rank tests or other nonparametric procedures. Lastly, it is not straightforward to extend this approach to classification and nonlinear models.

We thus provide a second possibility. The fast approximate version below is not fitting a model on each experimental setting separately as in Method I, but is just fitting one global model to all data and comparing the distribution of the residuals in each experimental setting. This is ignoring the sampling variability of the coefficient estimates but leads to a faster procedure.

1) For each S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} and e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}: (a) Fit a linear regression model on all data to get an estimate β^pred​(S)\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{pred}}(S) of the optimal coefficients using set SS of variables for linear prediction in regression. Let R=Y−X​β^pred​(S)R=Y-X\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{pred}}(S). (b) Test the null hypothesis that the mean of RR is identical for each set IeI_{e} and e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}, using a two-sample t-test for residuals in IeI_{e} against residuals in I−eI_{-{e}} and combing via Bonferroni correction across all e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. Furthermore, test whether the variances of RR are identical in IeI_{e} and I−eI_{-{e}}, using an F-test, and combine again via Bonferroni correction for all e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. Combine the two pp-values of equal variance and equal mean by taking twice the smaller of the two values. If the pp-value for the set SS is smaller than α\alpha, we reject the set SS. 2) As in the generic algorithm, using (13). 3) If we do reject a set SS we set Γ^S​(ℰ)=∅\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\emptyset. Otherwise, we set Γ^S​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}) to be the conventional (1−α)(1-\alpha)-confidence region for βpred​(S)\beta^{\mathrm{pred}}(S) when using all data simultaneously. For simplicity, we will use rectangular confidence regions, exactly as in step 3 of Method I.

Besides a computational advantage, the method can also easily be extended to nonlinear and logistic regression models. For logistic regression, one can test the residuals R=Y−f^​(X)R=Y-\hat{f}(X) for equal mean across the experimental settings, for example.

3.2 Data pooling

So far, we have assumed that the set ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of experimental settings is given and fixed. An experimental setting e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} can for example correspond to

  1. (i)

    observational data;

  2. (ii)

    a known intervention of a certain type at a known variable;

  3. (iii)

    a random intervention at an unknown and random location;

  4. (iv)

    observational data in a changed environment.

We have used data pooling in Methods I and II to get confidence intervals for the regression coefficients (which is not necessary but increases power in general). A justification of this pooling is in order. The joint distribution of (XS∗e,Ye)(X_{S^{*}}^{e},Y^{e}) will vary in general with e∈ℰe\in{\mathcal{E}}. Under Assumption 1, however, the conditional distribution Ye|XS∗eY^{e}\,|\,X_{S^{*}}^{e} is constant as a function of e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}, see Section 6.1. As long as our tests and confidence intervals require only an invariant conditional distribution for S∗S^{*} (which is the case for the procedures given above), we can pool data from various e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}.

To make it more precise, assume there is a set of countably many experimental settings or interventions 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} and (Xj,Yj)(X^{j},Y^{j}) follow a certain distribution FjF_{j} for each j∈𝒥{j}\in{\mathcal{J}}. Then each encountered experimental setting e{e} can be considered to be equivalent to a probability mixture distribution over the experimental settings in 𝒥{\mathcal{J}}, that is

Fe=∑j∈𝒥wje​Fj,F_{e}=\sum_{{j}\in{\mathcal{J}}}w_{j}^{e}F_{j},

where wjew^{e}_{j} corresponds to the probability that an observation under setting e{e} follows the distribution FjF_{j}. We can then pool two experimental settings e1{e}_{1} and e2{e}_{2}, for example, thereby creating a new experimental setting with the averaged weights (we1+we2)/2(w^{{e}_{1}}+w^{{e}_{2}})/2.

Pooling is a trade-off between identifiability and statistical power, assuming that Assumption 1 holds for the settings from 𝒥{\cal J}. The richer the set ℰ{\mathcal{E}} of experimental settings, the smaller the set Γ⁡(ℰ)\Gamma({\mathcal{E}}) of plausible causal coefficients will be and the larger the set of identifiable causal predictors S⁡(ℰ)S({\mathcal{E}}). By pooling data, we make the set of identifiable causal variables smaller, that is S⁡(ℰ)S({\mathcal{E}}) is shrinking as we reduce the number |ℰ||{\mathcal{E}}| of different settings. The trade-off can either be settled a-priori (for example if we know that we have “sufficiently” many observations in each known experimental setting, we would typically not pool data) or one can try various pooling procedures and combine all results, after adjusting the level α\alpha to account for the increased multiplicity of the associated testing problem. Section 4 discusses conditions on the interventions under which all true causal effects are identifiable.

3.3 Splitting purely observational data

In the case of purely observational data, the null hypothesis (4) is correct for γ=0\gamma=0 and S=∅S=\emptyset. Therefore, S⁡(ℰ)=∅S({\mathcal{E}})=\emptyset and S^​(ℰ)=∅\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\emptyset with high probability, i.e., our method stays conservative and does not make any causal claims.

In a reverse operation to data pooling across experiments, the question arises whether we can identify the causal predictors by artificially separating data into several blocks although the data have been generated under only one experimental setting (e.g. the data are purely observational). If the distribution is generated by a SEM (see Section 4.1), we may consider a variable U{U} that is not YY and known to be a non-descendant of the target variable YY, that is, there is no directed path from YY to U{U}, for example as it precedes YY chronologically. (This is similar as in an instrumental variable setting, see Section 5.) We may now split the data by conditioning on this variable U{U} or any function h⁡(U)h({U}). Our method then still has the correct coverage for any function h⁡(U)h({U}) as long as U{U} is a non-descendant of YY, because the conditional distribution of YY given its true causal predictors XS∗X_{S^{*}} does not change and for all zz in the image of hh,

Y|XS∗=𝑑Y|XS∗,h⁡(U)=zY\,|\,X_{S^{*}}\quad\overset{d}{=}\quad Y\,|\,X_{S^{*}},h({U})=z (19)

Note that U{U} might or might not be part of the set XS∗X_{S^{*}} but we expect the method to have more power if it is not. Equation (19) is a direct implication of the local Markov property that is satisfied for a SEM (Pearl, 2009, Theorem 1.4.1). The confidence intervals remain valid but the implication on (partial) identifiability of the causal predictors remains as an open question.

Even without data splitting, there might still be some directional information in the data set that is not exploited by our method; this may either be information in the conditional independence structure (Spirtes et al., 2000; Chickering, 2002), information from non-Gaussianity (Shimizu et al., 2006), nonlinearities (Hoyer et al., 2009; Peters et al., 2014; Bühlmann et al., 2014), equal error variances (Peters and Bühlmann, 2014) or shared information between regression function and target variable (Janzing et al., 2012). Our method does not exploit these sources of identifiability. We believe, however, that it might be possible to incorporate the identifiability based on non-Gaussianity or nonlinearity.

3.4 Computational requirements

The construction of the confidence regions for the set of plausible causal coefficients and the identifiable causal predictors requires to go through all possible sets of variables in step 1) of the procedures given above. The computational complexity of the brute force scheme seems to grow super-exponentially with the number of variables.

There are several aspects to this issue. Firstly, we often do not have to go through all sets of variables. If we are looking for a non-empty set S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}), it is worthwhile in general to start generating the confidence regions Γ^S​(ℰ)\hat{\Gamma}_{S}({\mathcal{E}}) for the empty set S=∅S=\emptyset, then for all singletons and so forth. If the empty set is not rejected, we can stop the search immediately, as then S^​(ℰ)=∅\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\emptyset. If the empty set is rejected, we can stop early as soon as we have accepted more than one set SS and the sets have an empty overlap (as S^=∅\hat{S}=\emptyset in this case no matter what other sets are accepted). The method can thus finish quickly if S^=∅\hat{S}=\emptyset. However, in a positive case (where we do hope to get a non-empty confidence set) we will still have to go through all sets of variables eventually. There are two options to address the computational complexity.

The first option is to limit a-priori the size of the set of causal predictors. Say we are willing to make the assumption that the set of causal variables is at most s<ps<p. Then we just have to search over all subsets of size at most ss and incur a computational complexity that grows like O⁡(ps)O(p^{s}) as a function of the number of variables.

A second option (which can be combined with the first one) is an adaptation of the confidence interval defined above, in which the number of variables is first reduced to a subset of small size that contains the causal predictors with high probability. Let B^⊆{1,…,p}\hat{B}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\} be, for the pooled data, an estimator of the variables with non-zero regression coefficient when using all variables as predictors. For example, B^\hat{B} could be the set of variables with non-zero regression coefficient with square-root Lasso estimation (Belloni et al., 2011), Lasso (Tibshirani, 1996) or boosting (Schapire et al., 1998; Friedman, 2001; Bühlmann and Yu, 2003) with cross-validated penalty parameter. If the initial screening is chosen such that the causal predictors are contained with high probability, P[S∗⊆B^]≥1−α,P\big[S^{*}\subseteq\hat{B}\big]\geq 1-\alpha, and we construct the confidence set S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) as above, but just letting SS be a subset of B^\hat{B} instead of {1,…,p}\{1,\ldots,p\}, it will have coverage at least 1−2​α1-2\alpha. Sufficient assumptions of such a coverage (or screening) condition are discussed in the literature (Bühlmann and van de Geer, 2011, e.g.). If the second option is combined with the first option, the computational complexity would then scale like O⁡(qs)O(q^{s}) instead of O⁡(ps)O(p^{s}), where qq is the maximal size of the set B^\hat{B} of selected variables. For the sake of simplicity, we will not develop this argument further here but rather focus on the identifiability results for the low(er)-dimensional case.

4 Identifiability results for structural equation models

The question arises whether the proposed confidence sets for the causal predictors can recover an assumed true set of causal predictors. Such identifiability issues are discussed next. Sections 4.1 and 4.2 describe possible data generating mechanisms and Section 4.3 provides corresponding identifiability results.

4.1 Linear Gaussian SEMs

We consider linear Gaussian structural equation models (SEMs) (Wright, 1921; Duncan, 1975, e.g.). We assume that each element e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} represents a different interventional setup. Let the first block of data (e=1e=1) always correspond to an “observational” (linear) Gaussian SEM. Here, a distribution over (X11,…,Xp+11)(X^{1}_{1},\ldots,X^{1}_{p+1}) is said to be generated from a Gaussian SEM if

Xj1=∑k≠jβj,k1X1k+ε1j,j=1,…,p+1,X_{j}^{1}=\sum_{k\neq j}\beta_{j,k}^{1}X^{1}_{k}+\varepsilon^{1}_{j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,p+1, (20)

with εj1​∼iid​𝒩​(0,σj2)\varepsilon_{j}^{1}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{j}^{2}), j=1,…,p+1j=1,\ldots,p+1. The corresponding directed graph is obtained by drawing arrows from variables Xk1X^{1}_{k} on the right-hand side of (20) with βj​k1≠0\beta_{jk}^{1}\neq 0 to the variables Xj1X^{1}_{j} of the left-hand side. This graph is assumed to be acyclic. Without loss of generality let us assume that Y1:=X11Y^{1}:=X^{1}_{1} is the target variable and we write X:=(X2,…,Xp+1)X:=(X_{2},\ldots,X_{p+1}). We further assume that all variables are observed; this assumption can be weakened, see Proposition 4 in Appendix B and Section 5.

The parents of YY are given by

𝐏𝐀⁡(Y)=𝐏𝐀⁡(1)={k∈{2,…,p+1}:β1,k1≠0}.{\mathbf{PA}}{(Y)}={\mathbf{PA}}{(1)}=\{k\in\{2,\ldots,{p+1}\}\,:\,\beta_{1,k}^{1}\neq 0\}.

Here, we adapt the usual notation of graphical models (Lauritzen, 1996, e.g.). For example, we write 𝐏𝐀⁡(j){\mathbf{PA}}{(j)}, 𝐃𝐄⁡(j){\mathbf{DE}}{(j)}, 𝐀𝐍⁡(j){\mathbf{AN}}{(j)} and 𝐍𝐃⁡(j){\mathbf{ND}}{(j)} for the parents, descendants, ancestors and non-descendants of XjX_{j}, respectively.

Let us assume that the other data blocks are generated by a linear SEM, too:

Xje=∑k≠jβj,keXek+εej,j=1,…,p+1,e∈ℰ.X_{j}^{e}=\sum_{k\neq j}\beta_{j,k}^{e}X^{e}_{k}+\varepsilon^{e}_{j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,p+1,\quad e\in{\mathcal{E}}. (21)

Assumption 1 states that the influence of the causal predictors remains the same under interventions, that is Ye=Xe​γ∗+ε11Y^{e}=X^{e}\gamma^{*}+\varepsilon^{1}_{1} for γ∗=(β1,21,…,β1,p+11)t\gamma^{*}=(\beta_{1,2}^{1},\ldots,\beta_{1,p+1}^{1})^{t} and ε1e​=𝑑​ε11\varepsilon^{e}_{1}\overset{d}{=}\varepsilon^{1}_{1} for e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. The other coefficients βj,ke\beta_{j,k}^{e} and noise variables εje\varepsilon^{e}_{j}, j≠1j\neq 1, however, may be different from the ones in the observational setting (20). Within this setting, we now define various sorts of interventions.

4.2 Interventions

We next discuss three different types of interventions that all lead to identifiability of the causal predictors for the target variable.

4.2.1 Do-interventions

These types of interventions correspond to the classical do-operation from Pearl (2009, e.g.). In the ee-th experiment, we intervene on variables 𝒜e⊆{2,…,p+1}\mathcal{A}^{e}\subseteq\{2,\ldots,p+1\} and set them to values aje∈ℝa^{e}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}, j∈𝒜ej\in\mathcal{A}^{e}. For the observational setting e=1e=1, we have 𝒜1=∅\mathcal{A}^{1}=\emptyset. We specify the model (21), for e≠1{e}\neq 1, as follows:

βj,ke={βj,k1 if ​j∉𝒜e0 if ​j∈𝒜e,\beta_{j,k}^{e}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\beta_{j,k}^{1}&\text{ if }j\notin\mathcal{A}^{e}\\ 0&\text{ if }j\in\mathcal{A}^{e},\end{array}\right.

and

εje​=𝑑​{εj1 if ​j∉𝒜eaje if ​j∈𝒜e.\varepsilon_{j}^{e}\overset{d}{=}\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\varepsilon_{j}^{1}&\text{ if }j\notin\mathcal{A}^{e}\\ a^{e}_{j}&\text{ if }j\in\mathcal{A}^{e}.\end{array}\right.

The do-interventions correspond to fixing the intervened variable at a specific value. The following two types of interventions consider “softer” forms of interventions which might be more realistic for certain applications.

4.2.2 Noise interventions

Instead of fixing the intervened variable at a specific value, noise interventions correspond to “disturbing” the variable by changing the distribution of the noise variable. This is an instance of what is sometimes called a “soft intervention” (Eberhardt and Scheines, 2007, e.g.). We now consider a kind of soft intervention, in which we scale the noise distributions of variables 𝒜e⊆{2,…,p+1}\mathcal{A}^{e}\subseteq\{2,\ldots,p+1\} by a factor AjeA^{e}_{j}, j∈𝒜ej\in\mathcal{A}^{e}. Alternatively, we may also shift the error distribution by a variable CjeC^{e}_{j}. More precisely, we specify the model in (21), for e≠1{e}\neq 1, as follows:

βj,ke=βj,k1for all ​j,\beta_{j,k}^{e}=\beta_{j,k}^{1}\quad\text{for all }j,

and

εje​=𝑑​{εj1 if ​j∉𝒜eAje​εj1 if ​j∈𝒜e, or εje​=𝑑​{εj1 if ​j∉𝒜eεj1+Cje if ​j∈𝒜e.\varepsilon_{j}^{e}\overset{d}{=}\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\varepsilon_{j}^{1}&\text{ if }j\notin\mathcal{A}^{e}\\ A^{e}_{j}\varepsilon_{j}^{1}&\text{ if }j\in\mathcal{A}^{e},\end{array}\right.\quad\text{ or }\quad\varepsilon_{j}^{e}\overset{d}{=}\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\varepsilon_{j}^{1}&\text{ if }j\notin\mathcal{A}^{e}\\ \varepsilon_{j}^{1}+C^{e}_{j}&\text{ if }j\in\mathcal{A}^{e}.\end{array}\right.

The factors AjeA^{e}_{j} and the shifts CjeC^{e}_{j} are considered as random but may be constant with probability one. They are assumed to be independent of each other and independent of all other random variables considered in the model except for XkeX_{k}^{e} for k∈𝐃𝐄⁡(j)k\in{\mathbf{DE}}{(j)}.

4.2.3 Simultaneous noise interventions

The noise interventions above operate on clearly defined variables 𝒜e\mathcal{A}^{e} which can vary between different experimental settings e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. In some applications, it might be difficult to change or influence the noise distribution at a single variable but instead one could imagine interventions that change the noise distributions at many variables simultaneously. As a third example, we thus consider a special case of the preceding Section 4.2.2, in which we pool all interventional experiments into a single data set. That is, |ℰ|=2|{\mathcal{E}}|=2 and, for all j∈{2,…,p+1}j\in\{2,\ldots,p+1\},

βj,ke=2=βj,ke=1\beta_{j,k}^{e=2}=\beta_{j,k}^{e=1} (22)

and

εje=2​=𝑑​Aj​εje=1 or εje=2​=𝑑​εje=1+Cj.\varepsilon_{j}^{e=2}\overset{d}{=}A_{j}\varepsilon_{j}^{e=1}\quad\text{ or }\quad\varepsilon_{j}^{e=2}\overset{d}{=}\varepsilon_{j}^{e=1}+C_{j}.

The random variables Aj≥0A_{j}\geq 0 are assumed to have a distribution that is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure with E​Aj2<∞{E}A_{j}^{2}<\infty and to be independent of all other variables and among themselves. The pooling can either happen explicitly or, as stated above, as we cannot control the target of the interventions precisely and a given change in environment might lead to changes in the error distributions in many variables simultaneously. As an example we mention gene knock-out experiments with off-target effects in biology (Jackson et al., 2003; Kulkarni et al., 2006, e.g.).

4.3 Identifiability results

The following Theorem 2 gives sufficient conditions for identifiability of the causal predictors. We then discuss some conditions under which the assumptions can or cannot be relaxed further below. Proofs can be found in Appendix F.

Theorem 2

Consider a (linear) Gaussian SEM as in (20) and (21) with interventions. Then, with S⁡(ℰ)S({\mathcal{E}}) as in (6), all causal predictors are identifiable, that is

S⁡(ℰ)=𝐏𝐀⁡(Y)=𝐏𝐀⁡(1)S({\mathcal{E}})={\mathbf{PA}}{(Y)}={\mathbf{PA}}{(1)} (23)

if one of the following three assumptions is satisfied:

  1. i)

    The interventions are do-interventions (Section 4.2.1) with aje≠E⁡(Xj1)a^{e}_{j}\neq{E}(X^{1}_{j}) and there is at least one single intervention on each variable other than YY, that is for each j∈{2,…,p+1}j\in\{2,\ldots,p+1\} there is an experiment ee with 𝒜e={j}\mathcal{A}^{e}=\{j\}.

  2. ii)

    The interventions are noise interventions (Section 4.2.2) with 1≠E​(Aje)2<∞1\neq{E}(A^{e}_{j})^{2}<\infty, and again, there is at least one single intervention on each variable other than YY. If the interventions act additively rather than multiplicatively, we require E​Cje≠0{E}C^{e}_{j}\neq 0 or 0<Var​Cje<∞0<{\mathrm{Var}}\,C^{e}_{j}<\infty.

  3. iii)

    The interventions are simultaneous noise interventions (Section 4.2.3). This result still holds if we allow changing linear coefficients βj,ke=2≠βj,ke=1\beta_{j,k}^{e=2}\neq\beta_{j,k}^{e=1} in (22) with (possibly random) coefficients βj,ke=2\beta_{j,k}^{e=2}.

The statements remain correct if we replace the null hypothesis (2.2) with its weaker version (17).

These are examples for sufficient conditions for identifiability but there may be many more. For example, one may also consider random coefficients or changing graph structures (only the parents of YY must remain the same).

Remark.

In general, the conditions given above are not necessary. The following remarks, however, provide two specific counter examples that show the necessity of some conditions.

  1. i)

    We cannot remove the condition aje≠E⁡(Xj1)a^{e}_{j}\neq{E}(X^{1}_{j}) from Theorem 2 i): the following SEMs correspond to observational data in experiment e=1e=1, interventional data with d​o​(X2=0)do(X_{2}=0) in experiment e=2e=2, and interventional data with d​o​(X3=0)do(X_{3}=0) in experiment e=3e=3:

    e\displaystyle e =1:\displaystyle=1: Y1\displaystyle\qquad Y^{1} =X21+X31+εY,\displaystyle=X_{2}^{1}+X_{3}^{1}+\varepsilon_{Y},\qquad X21\displaystyle X_{2}^{1} =ε2,\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{2},\qquad X31\displaystyle X_{3}^{1} =−X21+ε3,\displaystyle=-X_{2}^{1}+\varepsilon_{3},
    e\displaystyle e =2:\displaystyle=2: Y2\displaystyle\qquad Y^{2} =X22+X32+εY,\displaystyle=X_{2}^{2}+X_{3}^{2}+\varepsilon_{Y},\qquad X22\displaystyle X_{2}^{2} =0,\displaystyle=0,\qquad X32\displaystyle X_{3}^{2} =−X22+ε3,\displaystyle=-X_{2}^{2}+\varepsilon_{3},
    e\displaystyle e =3:\displaystyle=3: Y3\displaystyle\qquad Y^{3} =X23+X33+εY,\displaystyle=X_{2}^{3}+X_{3}^{3}+\varepsilon_{Y},\qquad X23\displaystyle X_{2}^{3} =ε2,\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{2},\qquad X33\displaystyle X_{3}^{3} =0,\displaystyle=0,

    with ε2\varepsilon_{2} and ε3\varepsilon_{3} having the same distribution. Then, we cannot identify the correct set of parents S∗={1,2}S^{*}=\{1,2\}. The reason is that even S=∅S=\emptyset leads to a correct null hypothesis (2.2).

  2. ii)

    If we only check the null hypothesis (17) instead of the stronger version (2.2) (namely whether the residuals have the same variance rather than the same distribution), the condition E​(Aje)2≠1{E}(A^{e}_{j})^{2}\neq 1 is essential. Consider a two-dimensional observational distribution from experiment e=1e=1 and an intervention distribution from experiment e=2e=2:

    e=1:\displaystyle e=1: X1\displaystyle X^{1} =εX,\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{X},\qquad Y1\displaystyle Y^{1} =X1+εY,\displaystyle=X^{1}+\varepsilon_{Y},
    e=2:\displaystyle e=2: X2\displaystyle X^{2} =A⋅εX,\displaystyle=A\cdot\varepsilon_{X},\qquad Y2\displaystyle Y^{2} =X2+εY,\displaystyle=X^{2}+\varepsilon_{Y},

    with E​(A)2=1{E}(A)^{2}=1 and εX,εY​∼iid​𝒩​(0,1)\varepsilon_{X},\varepsilon_{Y}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1). Then we cannot identify the correct set of parents 𝐏𝐀⁡(Y)={X}{\mathbf{PA}}{(Y)}=\{X\} because again S=∅S=\emptyset leads to the same residual variance and therefore a correct null hypothesis (17). If we use hypothesis (2.2), however, condition E​(Aje)2≠1{E}(A^{e}_{j})^{2}\neq 1 can be weakened (if densities exist), see the proof of Theorem 2 (iii).

In practice, we expect stronger identifiability results than Theorem 2. Intuitively, intervening on (some of) the ancestors of YY should be sufficient for identifiability in many cases. Note that the two counter-examples above are non-generic in the way that they violate faithfulness (Spirtes et al., 2000, e.g.). The following theorem shows for some graph structures (which need not to be known) that even one interventional setting with an intervention on a single node may be sufficient, as long as the data generating model is chosen “generically” (see Appendix A for an example).

Theorem 3

Assume a linear Gaussian SEM as in (20) and (21) with all non-zero parameters drawn from a joint density w.r.t. Lebesgue measure. Let Xk0X_{k_{0}} be a youngest parent of target variable Y=X1Y=X_{1}, that is there is no directed path from Xk0X_{k_{0}} to any other parent of YY. Assume further that there is an edge from any other parent of YY to Xk0X_{k_{0}}. Assume that there is only one intervention setting, where the intervention took place on Xk0X_{k_{0}}, that is |ℰ|=2|\mathcal{E}|=2 and 𝒜e=2={k0}\mathcal{A}^{e=2}=\{k_{0}\} (k0k_{0} does not need to be known).

Then, with probability one, all causal predictors are identifiable, that is

S⁡(ℰ)=𝐏𝐀⁡(Y)=𝐏𝐀⁡(1)S({\mathcal{E}})={\mathbf{PA}}{(Y)}=\mathbf{PA}({1})

if one of the following two assumptions is satisfied:

  1. i)

    The intervention is a do-intervention (Section 4.2.1) with ak0e=2≠E​Xk01a^{e=2}_{k_{0}}\neq{E}X^{1}_{k_{0}}.

  2. ii)

    The intervention is a noise intervention (Section 4.2.2) with 1≠E​(Ak0e=2)2<∞1\neq{E}(A^{e=2}_{k_{0}})^{2}<\infty or E​Ck0e=2≠0{E}C^{e=2}_{k_{0}}\neq 0, respectively.

It is, of course, also sufficient for identifiability if the interventional setting 𝒜e=2={k0}\mathcal{A}^{e=2}=\{k_{0}\} is just a member of a larger number of interventional settings. We anticipate that more identifiability results of similar type can be derived in specific settings. Theorem 3 shows that interving on the youngest parent can reveal the whole set of parents of the target variable so this intervention is in a sense the most informative intervention under the made assumptions. Intervening on descendants of YY will, in contrast, only rule out these variables as parents of YY. Some interventions are also completely non-informative; intervening on a variable that is independent of all other variables (including the target) will, for example, not help with identification of the set of parents of the target variable.

5 Instrumental and hidden variables with confounding

We now discuss an extension of the invariance idea that is suitable in the presence of hidden variables. Instrumental variables can sometimes be used when the causal relationship of interest is confounded and there are no randomised experiments available (Wright, 1928; Bowden and Turkington, 1990; Angrist et al., 1996; Didelez et al., 2010). For simplicity, let us assume that II is binary.

We assume that the SEM for a pp-dimensional predictor XX, a univariate target variable YY of interest and a qq-dimensional hidden variable HH can be written as

X\displaystyle X =f⁡(I,H,Y,η),\displaystyle=f(I,H,Y,\eta),
Y\displaystyle Y =X​γ∗+g⁡(H,ε),\displaystyle=X\gamma^{*}+g(H,\varepsilon), (24)

where γ∗\gamma^{*} is the unknown vector of causal coefficients, f,gf,g are unknown real-valued functions and η\eta and ε\varepsilon are random noise variables in pp dimensions and one dimension respectively. As it is commonly done for SEMs, we require the noise variables H,η,ε,IH,\eta,\varepsilon,I to be jointly independent. Figure 3 shows an example of a SEM that satisfies (24).

Again, we are interested in the causal coefficient γ∗\gamma^{*}. Because of the hidden variable HH, however, regressing YY on XX does not yield a consistent estimator for γ∗\gamma^{*}.

Two remarks on the model (24) are in place. First, the model requires that II has no direct effect on YY, which is standard assumption for instrumental variable models. For a discussion on why a violation of this assumption usually leads to no false conclusions (only a reduction in power), see Section 6.3. Second, the model (24) allows for feedback between XX and YY, that is the corresponding graph in a SEM is not required to be acyclic. If feedback exists, the solutions are typically understood to be stable equilibrium solutions of (24) but we will here only require that the solutions satisfy equations (24).

We can use II as an instrument in a classical sense and estimate γ∗\gamma^{*} by the following well-known two-stage least squares procedure (Angrist et al., 1996): first we estimate the influence of II on XX and then we regress YY on the predicted values of XX given II. For non-linear models one can use two-stage predictor substitution or two-stage residual inclusion; see (Terza et al., 2008) for an overview. If we strive for identification of γ∗\gamma^{*}, three limitations with this approach are:

  1. (i)

    The target YY is not allowed to be a parent of any component of XX, i.e., f⁡(I,H,Y,η)=f⁡(I,H,η)f(I,H,Y,\eta)=f(I,H,\eta). This also excludes the possibility of feedback between XX and YY.

  2. (ii)

    The conditional expectation E⁡(X|I)E(X\,|\,I) is not allowed to be constant for I∈{0,1}I\in\{0,1\}.

  3. (iii)

    The predictor XX has to be univariate for a univariate instrument II, that is p=1p=1 is required.

What happens if we interpret the two different values of II as two experimental settings? In other words: what happens if II plays the role of the indicator of environment (that we call EE at the end of Section 6.1) and we apply the method described above? We can define ℰ{\mathcal{E}} as two distinct environments by collecting all samples with I=0I=0 in the first environment and all samples with I=1I=1 in the second environment. Of course, another split into distinct environments is also possible and allowed as long as the split into distinct environments is not a function of YY, a descendant of YY or the hidden variables HH.

We stated in Proposition 1 that SEMs (with interventions) satisfy the assumptions of invariant predictions if there are no hidden variables between the target variable and the causal predictors. Because here there is the hidden variable HH we cannot justify our method using Proposition 1 (nor with Proposition 4 in general). However, the invariant prediction procedure (3) can be extended to cover models of the form (24) as these models fulfil

for all e∈ℰ:Xe\displaystyle\mbox{for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}:\quad X^{e} has an arbitrary distribution
Ye\displaystyle Y^{e} =Xe​γ∗+g⁡(He,εe),\displaystyle=X^{e}\gamma^{*}+g(H^{e},\varepsilon^{e}), (25)

with unknown causal coefficients γ∗∈ℝp\gamma^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and unknown function g:ℝq×ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{q}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}.

In the absence of hidden variables, the residuals Ye−Xe​γ∗Y^{e}-X^{e}\gamma^{*} are independent of the causal predictors XS∗e=Xsupp⁡(γ∗)eX^{e}_{S^{*}}=X^{e}_{\mathrm{supp}(\gamma^{*})} and have the same distribution across all environments. In the presence of hidden variables, we cannot require independence of the residuals and the causal predictors XS∗X_{S*} but can adapt the null hypothesis H0,SH_{0,S} in (5) to the weaker form

H0,S,ℎ𝑖𝑑𝑑𝑒𝑛​(ℰ):\displaystyle H_{0,S,\mathit{hidden}}({\mathcal{E}}):\quad ∃γ∈ℝp such that γk=0 if k∉S and\displaystyle\exists\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\text{ such that }\gamma_{k}=0\text{ if }k\notin S\mbox{ and }
the distribution of Ye−Xeγ is identical for all e∈ℰ.\displaystyle\mbox{ the distribution of }Y^{e}-X^{e}\gamma\mbox{ is identical for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}. (26)

Testing the null hypothesis (26) is computationally more challenging than for the corresponding null hypothesis in the absence of hidden confounders (5). In contrast to (5), we cannot attempt to find for a given set SS the vector γ\gamma by regressing YeY^{e} on XeX^{e}. The reason is that even if (26) holds, it does not require the residuals Ye−Xe​γY^{e}-X^{e}\gamma to be independent of Xsupp⁡(γ)eX_{\mathrm{supp}(\gamma)}^{e}.

Suppose nevertheless that we have a test for the null hypothesis H0,S,ℎ𝑖𝑑𝑑𝑒𝑛​(ℰ){H}_{0,S,\mathit{hidden}}({\mathcal{E}}) and define in analogy to (13) the estimated set of causal predictors as

S^(ℰ)=⋂S:H0,S,ℎ𝑖𝑑𝑑𝑒𝑛(ℰ) not rejectedS.\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})=\bigcap_{S:H_{0,S,\mathit{hidden}}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ not rejected}}S. (27)

Then the coverage property follows immediately in the following sense.

Proposition 2

Consider model (24) and let S∗={k:γk∗≠0}S^{*}=\{k:\gamma^{*}_{k}\neq 0\}. Suppose the test for H0,S,ℎ𝑖𝑑𝑑𝑒𝑛​(ℰ){H}_{0,S,\mathit{hidden}}({\mathcal{E}}) is conducted at level α\alpha and S^\hat{S} is defined as in (27). Then

P[S^(ℰ)⊆S∗]≥ 1−α.P[\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\subseteq S^{*}]\;\geq\;1-\alpha.

Proof. The hypothesis H0,S,ℎ𝑖𝑑𝑑𝑒𝑛​(ℰ)H_{0,S,\mathit{hidden}}({\mathcal{E}}) is obviously true for S∗S^{*} as Ye−Xe​γ∗=g⁡(He,εe)Y^{e}-X^{e}\gamma^{*}=g(H^{e},\varepsilon^{e}) and the distribution of g⁡(He,εe)g(H^{e},\varepsilon^{e}) is invariant across the environments e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}} (defined by II) as II is independent of HH and ε\varepsilon. □\square

The method has thus guaranteed coverage for model (24) even if the necessary assumptions (i)-(iii) for identification under a two-stage instrumental-variable approach are violated. The power of the procedure depends again on the type of interventions, the function class and the chosen test for the null hypothesis. We can ask for specific examples whether S^​(ℰ)=S∗\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})=S^{*} in the population limit.

Proposition 3

Assume as a special case of (24) a shift in the variance of XX under I=1I=1 compared to I=0I=0 observations:

X\displaystyle X =f⁡(H,η)+Z⋅1I=1\displaystyle=f(H,\eta)+Z\cdot 1_{I=1}
Y\displaystyle Y =X​γ∗+g⁡(H,ε),\displaystyle=X\gamma^{*}+g(H,\varepsilon), (28)

where the pp-dimensional mean-zero random variable ZZ is independent of H,ε,ηH,\varepsilon,\eta and II and has a full-rank covariance matrix. Then γ∗\gamma^{*} and S∗S^{*} are identifiable in a population sense. Specifically, if the test of H0,S,ℎ𝑖𝑑𝑑𝑒𝑛​(ℰ){H}_{0,S,\mathit{hidden}}({\mathcal{E}}) has power 1 against any alternative, then

P[S^(ℰ)=S∗]≥1−α.P[\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})=S^{*}]\geq 1-\alpha.

A proof is given in Appendix E. Note that the causal variables and coefficients can be identified for (28), even though the model violates the above-mentioned assumptions (ii) and (iii) for identifiability with a classical two-stage instrumental variable analysis: XX can be of arbitrary dimension even though the instrumental variable II is univariate and there is no shift in E⁡(X|I)E(X\,|\,I) between I=1I=1 and I=0I=0.

A further advantage of the invariance approach might be that no test for a weak influence of II on XX is necessary. A weak instrument can lead to amplification of biases in conventional instrumental variable regression (Hernán and Robins, 2006). With the invariance approach, the confidence intervals for γ∗\gamma^{*} are naturally wide in case of a weak influence of II on XX, leading to small sets S^\hat{S} of selected causal variables.

Ignoring the computational difficulties, this shows that the approach can be generalised to include hidden variables that violate assumption (ii) c) in Proposition 4, for example by replacing (5) with the null hypothesis (26). As a possible implementation of the general approach we must therefore test (26) for every set S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}. We are faced with a formidable computational challenge because the coefficients γ∗\gamma^{*} cannot be found by simple linear regression anymore. One possibility is to place a stricter constraint on the form of allowed interventions. For shifted soft interventions from Section 4.2.3, for example, such an approach is described in Rothenhäusler et al. (2015). For general interventions, we can test (26) in a brute-force way by testing the invariance of the distribution over a grid of γ\gamma-values. However, the computational complexity of this approach is exponential in the predictor dimension and it would be valuable to identify computationally more efficient ways of testing the null hypothesis (26).

6 Further extensions and model misspecification

6.1 Nonlinear models

We have shown an approach to obtain confidence intervals for the causal coefficients in linear models. We might be interested in identifying the set of causal predictors S∗S^{*} in the more general nonlinear setting (2). The equivalent null-hypothesis to (5) is then

H0,S,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛(ℰ):There exists ​g:ℝ|S|×ℝ→ℝ​ and ​εe​ such thatYe=g(XeS,εe),εe∼Fε and εe⟂⁣⟂XeS for all e∈ℰ.\displaystyle H_{0,S,\mathit{nonlin}}({\mathcal{E}}):\quad\begin{array}[]{rl}&\mbox{There exists }g:\mathbb{R}^{|S|}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\text{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\text{ such that}\\ &Y^{e}=g(X^{e}_{S},\varepsilon^{e}),\quad\varepsilon^{e}\sim F_{\varepsilon}\mbox{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}X^{e}_{S}\mbox{ for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}.\end{array}

It is interesting to note that SS satisfies (6.1) if and only if it satisfies

H0,S,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛(ℰ):∀e,f∈ℰ​ the conditional distributions ​Ye|XSe=x​ and ​Yf|XSf=xare identical for all ​x​ such that both cond. distr. are well-defined.\displaystyle H_{0,S,\mathit{nonlin}}({\mathcal{E}}):\quad\begin{array}[]{l}\forall{e},f\in{\mathcal{E}}\mbox{ the conditional distributions }Y^{e}\,|\,X_{S}^{e}=x\text{ and }Y^{f}\,|\,X_{S}^{f}=x\\ \text{are identical for all }x\text{ such that both cond.\ distr.\ are well-defined}.\end{array}

The “only if” part is immediate and for the “if” part we can use a similar idea as in (Peters et al., 2014, Prop. 9), for example, and choose a Uniform([0,1])([0,1])-distributed ε\varepsilon and g⁡(a,b)=ge​(a,b):=FYe|XSe=a−1​(b)g(a,b)=g^{e}(a,b):=F^{-1}_{Y^{e}\,|\,X_{S}^{e}=a}(b), where FYe|XSe=aF_{Y^{e}\,|\,X_{S}^{e}=a} is the cdf of Ye|XSe=aY^{e}\,|\,X_{S}^{e}=a.

As in the linear case, we can consider a SEM with environments corresponding to different interventions and, again, the parents of YY satisfy the null hypothesis. More precisely, we have the following remark.

Remark 2

Proposition 1 and Proposition 4 still hold if we replace linear SEMs (20) with nonlinear SEMs

Yj=fj(X𝐏𝐀⁡(j),εj),j=1,…,p+1Y_{j}=f_{j}(X_{{\mathbf{PA}}{(j)}},\varepsilon_{j}),\quad j=1,\ldots,p+1

and replace Assumption 1 with the assumption that there exists S∗S^{*} satisfying (6.1).

Proof. Again, the proof is immediate. Only the case with hidden variables requires an argument. From the SEM, we are given Ye=f⁡(XS0e,XSH0e,ε~e)Y^{e}=f(X_{S^{0}}^{e},X^{e}_{S_{H}^{0}},\tilde{\varepsilon}^{e}) with SH0S_{H}^{0} being the hidden parents of YY and (XSH0e,ε~e)​⟂⁣⟂​XS0e(X^{e}_{S_{H}^{0}},\tilde{\varepsilon}^{e})\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}X_{S^{0}}^{e}. We can then write Ye=g⁡(XS0,εe)Y^{e}=g(X_{S^{0}},\varepsilon^{e}) for a uniformly distributed εe\varepsilon^{e} that is independent of XS0X_{S^{0}} and g⁡(x,n):=Ff⁡(x,XSH0e,ε~e)−1​(n)g(x,n):=F^{-1}_{f(x,X^{e}_{S_{H}^{0}},\tilde{\varepsilon}^{e})}(n). The function gg does not depend on ee because XSH0eX^{e}_{S_{H}^{0}} and ε~e\tilde{\varepsilon}^{e} have the same distribution for all e∈ℰe\in{\mathcal{E}}. □\square

Assume we have a test for the null hypothesis H0,S,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛​(ℰ)H_{0,S,\mathit{nonlin}}({\mathcal{E}}). Then, testing all possible sets S⊆{1,…,p}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}, we can get a confidence set for S∗S^{*} in a similar way as in the linear setting (16) by

S^(ℰ):=⋂S:H0,S,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛​(ℰ)​ not rejectedS.\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\;:=\;\bigcap_{S:H_{0,S,\mathit{nonlin}}({\mathcal{E}})\text{ not rejected}}S. (33)

If all tests are conducted individually at level α\alpha, we have again the property that for any S∗S^{*} which fulfills (6.1) or (6.1), P⁡(S^​(ℰ)⊆S∗)≥1−αP(\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\subseteq S^{*})\geq 1-\alpha since the null hypothesis for S∗S^{*} will be accepted with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha.

Constructing suitable tests for (6.1) is easier if we are willing to assume that the function gg in (6.1) is additive in the noise component, that is

H0,S,𝑎𝑑𝑑𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑣𝑒(ℰ):there exists ​g:ℝ|S|→ℝ​ and ​εe​ such thatYe=g(XeS)+εe,εe∼Fε and εe⟂⁣⟂XeS for all e∈ℰ.H_{0,S,\mathit{additive}}({\mathcal{E}}):\quad\begin{array}[]{rl}&\mbox{there exists }g:\mathbb{R}^{|S|}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\text{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\text{ such that}\\ &Y^{e}=g(X^{e}_{S})+\varepsilon^{e},\quad\varepsilon^{e}\sim F_{\varepsilon}\mbox{ and }\varepsilon^{e}\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}X^{e}_{S}\mbox{ for all }{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}.\end{array} (34)

Then, we can construct tests for the null hypothesis (6.1) that are similar as in the linear case. Analogously to Method I in Section 3.1, we can perform nonlinear regression in each environment and test whether the regression functions are identical (e.g. Durot et al., 2013, for isotonic regression functions). As an alternative, we can also fit a regression model on the pooled data set and test whether the residuals have the same distribution in each environment, see Method II in Section 3.1.

We may also test (6.1) without assuming additivity of the noise component. This could be addressed by introducing an environment variable EE and then performing a conditional independence test for Y​⟂⁣⟂​E|XSY\mbox{${}\perp\mkern-11.0mu\perp{}$}E\,|\,X_{S}, see also Appendix C. The details of these approaches lie beyond the scope of this paper.

6.2 Interventions on the target variable and its causal mechanism

So far, we have assumed that the error distribution of the target variable is unchanged across all environments e∈ℰ{e}\in{\mathcal{E}}, see Assumption 1 for linear models. This precludes interventions on YY and precludes a change of the causal mechanism for the target variable. For the gene-knockout experiments mentioned in Section 2 and treated in detail in Section 7.2, we would for example know whether we have intervened on the target gene or not. In other situations, we might not be sure whether an intervention on the target variables occurred or not.

If interventions are sparse, other approaches are possible, too. For any given target variable YY, we might not be sure whether an intervention on YY occurred or not, but we can assume that an intervention on YY happened in at most V≪|ℰ|V\ll|{\mathcal{E}}| different environments, even if we do not know in which of the environments it occurred, see Kang et al. (2015) for a related setting in instrumental variable regression. The null hypothesis (6.1) in the general nonlinear case can then be weakened to

H0,S,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛′(ℰ):∃ℰ′⊆ℰ with |ℰ′|≥|ℰ|−V s.t. ∀e,f∈ℰ′ the cond. distr. Ye|XSe=xand ​Yf|XSf=x​ are identical ​∀x​ s.t. both cond. distr. are well-defined.H^{\prime}_{0,S,\mathit{nonlin}}({\mathcal{E}}):\;\begin{array}[]{l}\exists{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}\subseteq{\mathcal{E}}\mbox{ with }|{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}|\geq|{\mathcal{E}}|-V\text{ s.t. }\forall{e},f\in{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}\mbox{ the cond.\ distr.\ }Y^{e}\,|\,X_{S}^{e}=x\\ \text{and }Y^{f}\,|\,X_{S}^{f}=x\text{ are identical }\forall x\text{ s.t.\ both cond.\ distr.\ are well-defined}.\end{array} (35)

The null hypothesis H0,S∗,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛′H^{\prime}_{0,S^{*},\mathit{nonlin}} is then still true even when interventions happen on YY in some environments, where S∗S^{*} is the causal set of variables that satisfies the invariance assumption in the absence of interventions on YY. Any test for (6.1) can be extended as a test for the weaker null hypothesis (35) by testing all subsets ℰ′{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime} with |ℰ′|≥|ℰ|−V|{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}|\geq|{\mathcal{E}}|-V at level α\alpha, e.g. using a test for (6.1), and rejecting (35) only if we can reject all such subsets. We can then treat H0,S,𝑛𝑜𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛​(ℰ)H_{0,S,\mathit{nonlin}}({\mathcal{E}}) as being “accepted” if we find one subset ℰ′{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime} whose corresponding null hypothesis cannot be rejected.

6.3 Model misspecification

We have shown how the approach can be extended to cover hidden variables, nonlinear models and interventions on the target variable. The question arises how the original approach behaves if these model assumptions are violated but we use the original approach instead of the proposed extensions. We again write S^​(ℰ)\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}}) as in (16) as

S^(ℰ):=⋂S:H0,S​ not rejectedS.\hat{S}({\mathcal{E}})\;:=\;\bigcap_{S:H_{0,S}\text{ not rejected}}S.
